title: Proposal Data
description: Schema for proposals/proposal-data.json, the input of assemble-preview.js --type proposal and validate-proposal.js. A proposal is a decision record for one feature: the answer, the terrain it happens on, and one block per decision the feature forces, each with its options, its comparison and the pick with reasons that name the criterion they argue from.

meta.description: Document-level context printed in the title strip and the provenance comment

title.description: Document title, printed as the page H1 and the document title
examples: DIP-I-496: show role and permission for a logged-in user

ticket.description: Ticket or story id the proposal answers

date.description: Authoring date, YYYY-MM-DD, printed in the title strip. Never a render-time clock, so a re-render is byte-identical

apps.description: App slugs the ticket lives in, printed in the title strip

items.description: An app slug the vendored app-context knows

prompt.description: The request the document answers, kept in the provenance comment only
examples: Propose a design for this ticket: DIP-I-496

model.description: Model that authored the document, provenance comment only

skill.description: Always design-proposal; lets a reader tell this file from a flow-data.json

stage.description: Which stage of the pipeline this file is at. Absent means proposal, which is what every file authored before the evaluation stage existed is, so nothing needs touching. Only --evaluate writes "evaluation".

answer.description: One sentence: what we are doing. The first thing in the document, above the picks. Not a summary paragraph: if it needs two sentences, the second belongs in a decision
examples: Give Administration a per-item view of what a share exposed, and let an admin revoke one item without unsharing the product.

source.description: The ticket this proposal answers, as it arrived. Filled from pasted text today and by a fetcher later; nothing downstream cares which

id.description: The ticket id in that system

url.description: A link a reader can follow; omitted for a pasted ticket. Never rendered as a link, the document is offline

title.description: The ticket's own title, in its words
examples: Show role and permission for a logged-in user

body.description: The ticket text the proposal was written from, kept so a reader can check the proposal against it
examples: As a user I want to see which permission group I belong to.

context.description: Where the ticket lives and the question it asks, from the app-context and whatever the request attached

question.description: The design question in one sentence, as said in Step 1
examples: How does a logged-in user see their assigned role and permission group?

product.description: Facts about how the product handles this today, one line each: the anchor surface, the data model behind it, what an admin and a user see. Three to six is the useful range and six is the ceiling; fewer than three usually means the product read stopped early. Facts, not a paragraph

examples: A permission group is a Group record in Administration.
A user can belong to more than one group.

sources.description: Where the product read came from: app-context facts and attachments, one line each

items.description: One source, prefixed app-context: or attachment:

gap.description: One sentence naming what the substrate has no capture of, when the anchor surface is uncaptured; absent otherwise
examples: The account dropdown has no capture in app-context.

scope.description: What the proposal is for and what it deliberately leaves out. Non-goals are what stops a reviewer scoping the work sideways; they are as load-bearing as the goals.

goals.description: One to four things the change must achieve, each in one line, drawn from the ticket rather than invented

examples: A user can read their permission group without leaving the dropdown.

nonGoals.description: One to four things this change deliberately does not do, each in one line; the reviewer reads these to know what not to ask for

examples: Editing a permission group from the dropdown; assignment stays in Administration.

research.description: What comparable products do, bounded to five findings with a source each; always present, and honest when it did not run

ran.description: true when the web research ran; false when it was turned off or unavailable

findings.description: At most five findings (validator-enforced); empty when ran is false

claim.description: One sentence in the reader's words
examples: Role sits under the name as a secondary identity signal, never above it.

source.description: The product or article the claim comes from, as text (the document loads nothing)
examples: SaaS Permissions and Roles UX Patterns, SaaSUI Design

skippedBecause.description: Required when ran is false (validator-enforced): why the research did not run
examples: no web search in this session

breadboard.description: The terrain: the places this feature touches and what connects to what. Required when the places span more than one app, omitted entirely for a single place, optional in between. Never a screen design

places.description: Two to six places, each a box on the diagram

items.description: One place: a surface that exists, or one this feature adds

id.description: Slug unique among places; the key connections name

name.description: The place in the product's words, two or three words

app.description: App slug from the vendored app-context, drawn as the box's first line

affordances.description: One to five things a person can do here, or that is true here; one short line each

items.description: One affordance in a few words

row.description: 0-based grid row; omitted means every place on one row in declaration order

col.description: 0-based grid column; omitted means declaration order across the row

isNew.description: true when this feature adds the place; drawn dashed and in the brand colour

connections.description: What reaches what. Drawn as orthogonal arrows routed through the gutters between the boxes

from.description: A place id, or an affordance as <placeId>/<n> with n the 1-based index of the affordance the line leaves from

label.description: Two or three words on the line, printed uppercase

isNew.description: true when this feature adds the connection; drawn dashed and in the brand colour

decisions.description: One to four decisions the feature forces. Each is self-contained: its own question, options, comparison and pick. A simple ticket has one, which is the old single-decision document exactly

id.description: Slug unique in the file; the anchor a reader and the flow bridge address the decision by

question.description: The decision as a question in one sentence
examples: How does a user see which group they belong to?

options.description: Two to four options, each drawn inside its anchor surface; four is the ceiling the row budget can draw side by side

items.description: One option for one decision: a name, an anchor, two lines, a verdict, a drawing and the screen list a flow would render

id.description: Slug unique inside its decision; the key of its comparison cells and the target of pick.optionId

name.description: Short name printed on the card and in the comparison header

anchor.description: The surface the option is drawn inside; usually the same for every option in a decision

app.description: App slug from the vendored app-context; the assembler renders that app's header strip

surface.description: The product surface in the product's words

whatItIs.description: One line: what the option is
examples: Each assigned group as a small pill under the name.

breaksWhen.description: One line: the case where it breaks
examples: A user in many groups: the pills wrap into a paragraph.

verdict.description: A few words printed as a tag on the card
examples: Scans well, scales to a few groups

screen.description: The drawing: a Fat Marker fragment rendered under the anchor app's header strip. Every option in a decision renders at the same width, which the assembler computes; width here is the author's intent

width.description: Intended drawing width in px, 240 to 720 (validator-enforced). The assembler equalises within a decision, so a wider sibling raises this one

html.description: The Fat Marker fragment: fm-* classes and --fm-* tokens only, drawn in flow, no script, no external loads; see references/design-proposal/document-authoring.md

notes.description: At most three phrases annotating the drawing, each pointing at what the reader should notice

items.description: One annotation, a phrase not a sentence

screens.description: The screen list a flow of this option would render, in generate-flow's screen-list shape; one to four entries

items.description: One screen the flow would author

entity.description: An app-context entity slug, or null when the screen has no primary entity

note.description: What this option changes on the screen, for the flow's author
examples: The account menu shows the role badge under the name.

comparison.description: The options against criteria that come from the ticket's goal, the product's facts, or cost

criteria.description: Rows of the comparison table, in reading order. Three to six: the ceiling is enforced here, and a table of fewer than three rows is a validator finding, because it does not separate the options, which is what it is for

items.description: One criterion and where it comes from

id.description: Slug unique among this decision's criteria; the key of the cells and the target of a reason's criterionId

cells.description: Keyed by option id, then criterion id; each value is { text, tone } with tone one of good, mixed, bad (validator-enforced)

pick.description: Which option wins this decision, argued from its own comparison, and what it costs

optionId.description: The id of the winning option in this decision (validator-checked)

reasons.description: Two to four reasons. Each names the criterion it argues from, which is what makes the argument traceable rather than taste

items.description: One reason and the comparison row it argues from

criterionId.description: A criterion id from this decision's comparison (validator-checked). A reason that cannot name one is taste, or belongs in cost

text.description: One line: why this option wins that row
examples: One group is the common case, so the pill answers the question at a glance.

cost.description: What ships with this pick: the risk, the debt or the work it takes on. Required, because it is the thing a reader is actually evaluating
examples: A user in five groups sees a wrapped row until the truncation lands.

blocker.description: One sentence: a question that would change this pick if answered differently. Absent when nothing blocks. Not an open question, which by definition does not change a pick
examples: Whether a catalog can be scoped per group decides if one revoke is enough.

openQuestions.description: At most four things the proposal does not settle and that do NOT change any pick: a rabbit hole is a detail of a chosen option worth flagging so nobody falls in, an open question is something a reader has to decide later. Anything that would change a pick is that decision's blocker instead. Omit the field when there are none; never invent one.

items.description: One rabbit hole or one open question

kind.description: Which of the two this is

text.description: One or two sentences, in the reader's words
examples: Truncating a long group list needs a hover affordance the dropdown does not have today.

change.description: What this proposal changes, on each side. At least one side must say something (validator-enforced): a change that changes nothing anywhere is not a proposal

adminSide.description: What changes for administrators, one or two lines
examples: One optional Display name field on the group form.

userSide.description: What changes for users, one or two lines
examples: The display name surfaces under the name in the account menu.

latitude.description: One line telling the reader how much of this is fixed: the drawings are one way to solve the question, not the only way. Closes the document
examples: The drawings show one way to place these; the team has latitude on the layout, not on the picks.
